CausalChain: Chronic liver damage -> altered bile acid metabolism and increased intestinal permeability -> dysbiosis of the gut microbiome -> aberrant microbial metabolite and inflammatory mediator production -> impaired hepatocyte function (reduced albumin synthesis and bilirubin clearance) -> worsened ALBI grade -> poorer HCC prognosis and reduced efficacy of systemic therapies || Precision microbiome modulation (via targeted probiotics and engineered consortia) -> restoration of bile acid homeostasis (via FXR/TGR5 signaling) and reduction of inflammation -> improved hepatocyte function -> improved ALBI grade -> enhanced clinical outcomes and systemic therapy efficacy
Hypothesis: We hypothesize that in patients with hepatocellular carcinoma, the application of a precision-guided gut microbiome intervention—utilizing targeted probiotic strains or engineered microbial consortia selected through comprehensive metagenomic, metabolomic, and immunologic profiling—will restore disrupted bile acid homeostasis by enhancing FXR/TGR5-mediated signaling pathways. This restoration will reduce systemic and hepatic inflammation, thereby improving hepatocyte synthetic function, as evidenced by enhanced albumin production and bilirubin clearance (improved ALBI grade). Ultimately, this improved hepatic function will lead to improved clinical outcomes and increased responsiveness to systemic therapies. Furthermore, the use of real-time biomarker monitoring will allow for dynamic patient stratification and optimization of therapeutic regimens.
Abstract: This study proposes that precision modulation of the gut microbiome can restore the gut–liver axis homeostasis in patients with hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) through a targeted, multi-omics guided intervention. Specifically, by leveraging state‐of‐the‐art metagenomic profiling and advanced metabolomic and immunologic biomarker assays, we aim to identify and administer tailored probiotic strains (or engineered microbial consortia) that specifically enhance bile acid signaling via FXR/TGR5 pathways. This targeted microbial intervention seeks to counteract the cascade of chronic liver damage that leads to altered bile acid metabolism, increased intestinal permeability, and resultant dysbiosis. By restoring bile acid homeostasis and mitigating inflammatory mediator release, hepatocyte function—assessed by improved albumin synthesis and bilirubin clearance as captured by ALBI grading—should be enhanced. Improved liver synthetic capacity is anticipated to correlate with better clinical outcomes and an increased efficacy of systemic therapies in HCC patients. The integration of precision microbiome therapies with advanced monitoring techniques represents a novel, feasible strategy to address the unmet therapeutic challenges in HCC management.
Orignal_vs_New: The original hypothesis suggested that modulating the gut microbiome via generic interventions (probiotics, prebiotics, or FMT) could improve hepatocyte function by normalizing bile acid metabolism and reducing inflammation to improve ALBI grade. The revised hypothesis maintains the fundamental causal chain—chronic liver damage affecting bile acid metabolism leading to dysbiosis and impaired hepatocyte function—but introduces greater specificity and practical implementability. It now incorporates advanced technologies such as metagenomic and metabolomic profiling to identify specific microbial targets, specifies the role of FXR/TGR5 signaling in bile acid homeostasis, and proposes tailored microbial interventions. This revised approach addresses the need for precise mechanistic pathways and patient stratification, thereby enhancing the novelty, logical coherence, and translational potential of the original concept.
